passages.t: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Then: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (verse 1).

The sky is pictured as a voice that never stops. “Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge” (verse 2). Yet it uses no words: “Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard, their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world” (verses 3-4).

Then the poet turns to the sun. God “has pitched a tent for the sun” (verse 4). Each morning it comes out “Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber, like a champion rejoicing to run his course” (verse 5). It crosses the whole sky, and “nothing is deprived of its warmth” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 19 is a hymn in two halves: the sky (verses 1 to 6) and God's law (verses 7 to 14). Some scholars think the halves were once two poems joined together. Others think the psalm was written as one, since the halves balance each other, both about speech and light. C. S. Lewis, in Reflections on the Psalms (1958), called it the greatest poem in the Psalter and one of the greatest lyrics in the world.

The first hearers lived among peoples who worshipped the sun. In Mesopotamia the sun god, Shamash, was also the god of justice, who saw everything. Psalm 19 does not argue with that belief. It simply puts the sun in its place. The sun is not a god. It lives in a tent God set up. It runs the track God set for it. Its glory points past itself.

The pictures in verse 5 are joyful. A bridegroom came out of the wedding room glowing. A champion was a strong runner, eager for the race.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans and gives it a new turn. He uses the sky's worldwide voice as a picture of the message about Christ reaching every land: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10:18).

He also says that creation itself makes God known: “His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship” (Romans 1:20). John's Gospel speaks of “The true Light who gives light to every man” (John 1:9).
passages.hard:
Does the psalm teach that the sun goes round the earth? It speaks the way every poet speaks, and the way we still speak when we say ‘sunrise’ and ‘sunset’. It describes the sky as the eye sees it. Its point is not how the heavens move but who made them.

Nor does the psalm settle questions about the age of the earth or how living things came to be. Christians hold different views on those, and Psalm 19 does not take a side. What it says is that the sky is not silent. It speaks of God to everyone, in every language.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks you to look up. When did you last stand under a night sky and let it speak?

It also asks whether you have heard what the sky says. Its speech has no words, but it is clear: someone made this, and he is glorious.

passages.t: ‘The Law of the LORD is perfect’, and ‘my Rock and my Redeemer’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm turns from the sky to God's word. “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple” (verse 7). Six lines give God's word six names and say what each one does. It brings joy to the heart and “light to the eyes” (verse 8).

“They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb” (verse 10).

Then the light turns inward. “Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (verse 12). He asks to be kept from “willful sins” (verse 13).

The psalm closes with a prayer many still use before they speak or preach: “May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
In the first half God is called ‘God’ once. In the second half he is called ‘the LORD’, his personal name, seven times. The God whose glory the sky shows to everyone is the God who gave his word to Israel by name.

‘Law’ is torah. It means more than rules. It means teaching, the instruction of a loving father. That is why the psalmist can call it sweet. Gold and honey were the most precious and the sweetest things he knew.

Notice the link between the halves. Nothing is ‘deprived of its warmth’ under the sun (verse 6). In the same way, nothing in a person is hidden from God's word. The sun reaches every corner of the earth. The word reaches every corner of the heart.

‘Redeemer’ in verse 14 is go'el. In Israel the go'el was the near relative who stepped in to rescue a family member: buying back land or freeing someone sold into slavery. Boaz was Ruth's go'el (Ruth 4:14 calls him a ‘kinsman-redeemer’).
passages.later:
Paul agrees that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12). Jesus answered temptation with Scripture: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Hebrews says God's word “judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12), the work verse 12 asks for.

John's Gospel joins the two halves of the psalm in one person. The light of the world and the Word of God are Jesus: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14).
passages.hard:
‘Hidden faults’ (verse 12). How can you be forgiven for sins you do not even know about?

The psalmist knows that the heart hides things from itself. He does not try to dig them all out first. He asks God to cleanse what he cannot see. Israel's law made a difference between sins done without knowing and sins done on purpose (Numbers 15:27-30), ‘willful sins’ (verse 13). He asks for mercy for the first and protection from the second.

This is not a call to anxious self-examination. It is the opposite. You hand to God what you cannot fully know about yourself, and trust him with it.
passages.asks:
Verse 10 asks what you treat as precious and sweet. Is God's word gold to you, or homework?

Try praying verse 14 before you speak today: in a hard meeting, at the dinner table, before you post something. It is a short prayer. It covers both what you say and what you think.
